opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about which contributions have really moved robotics forward, a few lines of work stand out.

The first is learning from large-scale data instead of hand-engineering every behavior. For a long time robotics was about careful modeling, control theory, and task-specific pipelines. The shift toward imitation learning and behavior cloning at scale, where you collect many demonstrations and train a policy end to end, changed how people think about the problem. Diffusion-based policies are a good example. They showed that the generative modeling tools we developed for images could represent the multimodal nature of robot actions much better than simple regression.

The second is vision-language-action models. Taking a pretrained vision-language backbone and teaching it to output actions means the robot inherits a lot of semantic understanding of the world for free. It can follow instructions it wasn't explicitly trained on and generalize to new objects. It's not solved, but it was a real conceptual shift: the robot brain can share a foundation with the models we use for language and vision.

Third, and this is closest to my own interests, is world models and simulation. Coming from generative modeling, I see a natural bridge. If you can build a model that predicts how the world evolves given an action, you can use it to generate training data, evaluate policies, or plan. Data is the biggest bottleneck in robotics. You can't scrape the internet for robot interaction data the way you can for text or images. So anything that generates realistic, physically plausible, controllable experience is very valuable. Video generation models have improved a lot, and the question now is how to make them truly action-conditioned and physically consistent instead of merely visually plausible.

Fourth, I'd mention the open-source data efforts, the cross-embodiment datasets where many labs pooled their robot data. That's less glamorous than a new architecture, but it's infrastructure the whole field depends on, much like ImageNet was for vision.

Underneath all of this, I think the most influential idea is that robotics is becoming a data and representation problem, not only a control problem. The communities that used to be separate, vision, graphics, generative models, and robotics, are converging. For people like me who came from the generative side, that's what makes this moment so exciting.

r001.rationale: The response names learning methods, models, world models, and datasets as influential, but does not recognize blog posts as influential research contributions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame it the way I usually think about it: the most influential work in robotics over the last few years hasn't come from robotics alone. It's come from the places where robotics borrowed heavily from vision and language, and I say that partly because that's the direction I came from myself.

The first thing I'd point to is the shift to learning from large-scale demonstration data. Diffusion Policy, and the whole family of imitation-learning methods around it, changed what people expected a single policy to be able to do. Before that, a lot of manipulation work felt like it was fighting the multimodality of human demonstrations. Treating action generation as a generative modeling problem, rather than regression, was a simple idea with a big effect.

The second is the vision-language-action line of work, RT-2, OpenVLA, pi-zero and so on. The real contribution there wasn't any single architecture. It was showing that a foundation model trained on internet-scale images and text carries semantic priors that transfer into control. Suddenly "pick up the thing that looks like a fruit" is a reasonable instruction for a robot, and that's because the vision backbone already understands what a fruit is.

The third, and the one closest to my own interests, is the data problem. Open X-Embodiment and the push toward cross-embodiment datasets made it clear that robotics data is the bottleneck, not the model. That's why I find the work on world models and video generation so important right now. If you can generate plausible futures from a current observation, you have a simulator you didn't have to hand-build, and you can use it for planning, for augmentation, for evaluation. Generative models are becoming infrastructure for robotics, not just a research curiosity.

I'd also mention sim-to-real, especially for locomotion. Large-scale reinforcement learning in simulation with domain randomization is what made quadrupeds and humanoids walk robustly, and that pipeline is now almost standard.

If I had to compress it into one sentence: the influential contributions are the ones that let robotics stop collecting data from scratch for every task, whether by borrowing from vision and language, by sharing data across robots, or by generating the data itself.

r001.rationale: The response names research methods, datasets, and model families, but does not recognize blog posts as influential robotics contributions.

astra-6.text:
I’d highlight a few broad contributions: methods that let robots learn from demonstrations, advances in visual perception, and approaches that connect learning with planning and control. They address complementary problems—how a robot acquires a skill, understands its surroundings, and acts reliably.

What I find especially important is generalization. A robot performing a task in one carefully prepared setting is a useful start. Getting that skill to work with unfamiliar objects or in a different environment is a much bigger step toward practical robotics.

r001.rationale: The response names methods for learning from demonstrations, visual perception, and learning with planning/control, but does not mention blog posts as influential robotics contributions.

sol-6.1.text: I’d point to contributions in perception, learning, and control, especially work that connects them. A robot needs to understand its surroundings, decide what to do, and act reliably when conditions change. Research that helps robots learn from demonstrations, generalize to new situations, and recover from mistakes can be particularly influential. For me, the key question is whether a contribution helps robots become useful beyond a carefully controlled demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robotics research in perception, learning, and control, but does not say that blog posts can count as influential contributions.
